topics.name: Describing Material Properties
topics.description: Different materials respond differently to bending, stretching and contact with water. Properties help people select materials for a purpose.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 9–10, Phase 1 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: comparing material properties.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Fabric is more likely to bend without breaking; compare the materials safely to check.
misconceptions: All solid materials behave in the same way when bent.
topics.question: A card must bend without breaking. Which would you test first, fabric or a brittle cracker?
topics.answer: Fabric is more likely to bend without breaking; compare the materials safely to check.
topics.explanation: Different materials respond differently to bending, stretching and contact with water. Properties help people select materials for a purpose.
hints: Consider what happens when each material bends.
Which material can change shape without crumbling?
topics.activity: Compare safe samples of paper and fabric by bending them gently and describing what happens.

topics.name: Pushes, pulls and movement
topics.description: A push or pull can change how an object moves. The effect depends on the interaction and the situation.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 9–10, Phase 1 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: pushes, pulls and movement.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: A push from the hand changed the car's motion.
misconceptions: Objects can begin moving without any interaction.
topics.question: A stationary toy car starts moving when pushed. What changed its motion?
topics.answer: A push from the hand changed the car's motion.
topics.explanation: A push or pull can change how an object moves. The effect depends on the interaction and the situation.
hints: What touched the car?
Was the car already moving before the push?
topics.activity: On a clear floor, give a toy car a gentle push, observe its movement and describe the interaction.

topics.name: Sounds and vibrations
topics.description: Many sounds begin when an object vibrates. A vibrating object can make the surrounding air vibrate too.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 9–10, Phase 1 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: sounds and vibrations.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It vibrates, moving back and forth.
misconceptions: A sound-making object is always completely still.
topics.question: A stretched rubber band makes a sound when plucked. What can you see it doing?
topics.answer: It vibrates, moving back and forth.
topics.explanation: Many sounds begin when an object vibrates. A vibrating object can make the surrounding air vibrate too.
hints: Look carefully just after the band is plucked.
Describe the repeated movement.
topics.activity: Pluck a loosely stretched rubber band gently with adult supervision; watch and listen without pulling it towards anyone.

topics.name: Comparing life cycles
topics.description: Living things grow and reproduce, but their life cycles can have different stages and forms.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 11–12, Phase 1 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: comparing life cycles.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The chrysalis stage follows the caterpillar.
misconceptions: Every living thing follows exactly the same life cycle.
topics.question: A butterfly develops from an egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult. What follows the caterpillar?
topics.answer: The chrysalis stage follows the caterpillar.
topics.explanation: Living things grow and reproduce, but their life cycles can have different stages and forms.
hints: Find the stage after caterpillar in the sequence.
It comes before the adult butterfly.
topics.activity: Arrange drawings of a butterfly's stages in order and compare them with the life cycle of a flowering plant.

topics.name: Living things and their habitats
topics.description: A habitat provides living things with conditions and resources they need, though different organisms need different things.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 11–12, Phase 1 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: living things and their habitats.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They have different needs and are suited to different conditions; a fish needs water to live.
misconceptions: All living things need exactly the same habitat.
topics.question: Why might a fish and a garden snail live in different places?
topics.answer: They have different needs and are suited to different conditions; a fish needs water to live.
topics.explanation: A habitat provides living things with conditions and resources they need, though different organisms need different things.
hints: Think about where each animal gets what it needs.
What environment does the fish need?
topics.activity: Observe two habitats from a safe distance and list a visible living thing and one condition in each.

topics.name: Grouping living things by features
topics.description: Scientists can group organisms by observable features while recognising that plants, animals and fungi are different kinds of living things.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 11–12, Phase 1 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: grouping living things by features.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They could compare visible plant structures, such as leaves or fronds, while using a reliable identification guide.
misconceptions: Everything growing outdoors is a plant.
topics.question: A child groups a fern with a tree because both are plants. What shared feature or evidence might they look for?
topics.answer: They could compare visible plant structures, such as leaves or fronds, while using a reliable identification guide.
topics.explanation: Scientists can group organisms by observable features while recognising that plants, animals and fungi are different kinds of living things.
hints: Look at the organisms, not just where they are found.
What visible plant structures could you compare?
topics.activity: Look at photographs of a fern, tree and mushroom, and suggest a safe grouping based on visible features.

topics.name: States of matter and change
topics.description: Solids, liquids and gases differ in how they occupy space. Changing state by heating or cooling does not necessarily produce a new substance.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 14–15, Phase 2 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: states of matter and change.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: No. The water has changed state from solid to liquid.
misconceptions: Melting automatically creates a different substance.
topics.question: Ice melts into water. Has a new substance necessarily been made?
topics.answer: No. The water has changed state from solid to liquid.
topics.explanation: Solids, liquids and gases differ in how they occupy space. Changing state by heating or cooling does not necessarily produce a new substance.
hints: What was the ice made of?
What liquid results when it melts?
topics.activity: Observe an ice cube melting in a dish and describe how its shape and state change.

topics.name: Mass and volume
topics.description: Mass and volume describe different properties: how much matter an object contains and how much space it occupies.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 14–15, Phase 2 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: mass and volume.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: No. Equal volume does not guarantee equal mass.
misconceptions: Objects with equal volume always have equal mass.
topics.question: Two same-sized containers are filled with water and dry leaves. Must their contents have the same mass?
topics.answer: No. Equal volume does not guarantee equal mass.
topics.explanation: Mass and volume describe different properties: how much matter an object contains and how much space it occupies.
hints: The containers occupy the same space.
Does that require the contents to be equally heavy?
topics.activity: Compare the mass of equal-volume containers holding different safe materials, and record the results.

topics.name: Water moving through Earth systems
topics.description: Water moves between Earth's surface and the atmosphere through processes including evaporation, condensation and precipitation.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 14–15, Phase 2 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: water moving through earth systems.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Condensation.
misconceptions: Water disappears permanently when it evaporates.
topics.question: Water vapour cools and forms tiny droplets. What process has occurred?
topics.answer: Condensation.
topics.explanation: Water moves between Earth's surface and the atmosphere through processes including evaporation, condensation and precipitation.
hints: Is the water changing from gas to liquid or liquid to gas?
Cooling water vapour forms liquid droplets.
topics.activity: Draw and label a simple water cycle, then describe where each labelled change occurs.

topics.name: Seeds and dispersal
topics.description: Seeds can be dispersed in different ways, including by wind and animals, helping plants spread to suitable places.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 16–17, Phase 2 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: seeds and dispersal.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The structure can help wind carry the seed away from the parent plant.
misconceptions: All seeds move away from a parent plant in the same way.
topics.question: A seed has a light wing-like structure. How might that help it spread?
topics.answer: The structure can help wind carry the seed away from the parent plant.
topics.explanation: Seeds can be dispersed in different ways, including by wind and animals, helping plants spread to suitable places.
hints: What can move light objects through the air?
Think about the seed's wing-like shape.
topics.activity: Observe pictures of different seeds and match each structure to a plausible dispersal mechanism.

topics.name: Connections in a food web
topics.description: Food webs show feeding relationships; a change to one population can affect other connected organisms.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 16–17, Phase 2 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: connections in a food web.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It may have less food available, which could affect its population; other food sources and conditions also matter.
misconceptions: A food web shows no relationships between living things.
topics.question: If a plant population decreases, what might happen to an animal that depends on it for food?
topics.answer: It may have less food available, which could affect its population; other food sources and conditions also matter.
topics.explanation: Food webs show feeding relationships; a change to one population can affect other connected organisms.
hints: What does the animal eat?
Could another food source change the outcome?
topics.activity: Draw a simple food web using three fictional organisms and explain one possible effect of a change.

topics.name: Body systems working together
topics.description: Body systems have different functions and interact to support the whole organism.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 16–17, Phase 2 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: body systems working together.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Breathing brings oxygen into the body and circulation transports it to tissues.
misconceptions: Each body system works completely independently of all others.
topics.question: Why do breathing and circulation work together during movement?
topics.answer: Breathing brings oxygen into the body and circulation transports it to tissues.
topics.explanation: Body systems have different functions and interact to support the whole organism.
hints: What enters the lungs from the air?
How can oxygen travel from the lungs to other parts of the body?
topics.activity: Draw a simple pathway from lungs to bloodstream to muscles and explain it in your own words.

topics.name: The Particle Model
topics.description: A particle model can help explain why solids keep their shape while gases spread out. Models simplify reality to explain observable behaviour.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–20, Phase 3 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: particle models of states.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Gas particles are far apart and move around, spreading through the available space.
misconceptions: Gas particles disappear because they cannot be seen.
topics.question: Why does a gas spread through its container in a simple particle model?
topics.answer: Gas particles are far apart and move around, spreading through the available space.
topics.explanation: A particle model can help explain why solids keep their shape while gases spread out. Models simplify reality to explain observable behaviour.
hints: Compare the spacing of particles in a gas and a solid.
What does movement allow gas particles to do?
topics.activity: Use dots on paper to model a solid and a gas, then identify what the model does and does not show.

topics.name: Separating Mixtures
topics.description: A mixture contains substances that can often be separated using differences in physical properties, such as particle size or solubility.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–20, Phase 3 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: separating mixtures by properties.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Filter it so the water passes through and the sand remains in the filter.
misconceptions: Every mixture can only be separated by a chemical reaction.
topics.question: How could a mixture of sand and water be separated?
topics.answer: Filter it so the water passes through and the sand remains in the filter.
topics.explanation: A mixture contains substances that can often be separated using differences in physical properties, such as particle size or solubility.
hints: The sand does not dissolve in water.
What material could allow water through but retain the sand?
topics.activity: Filter a small clean sand-and-water mixture using paper and describe which property made separation possible.

topics.name: Planning a fair test
topics.description: A fair test changes one factor deliberately while measuring an outcome and keeping relevant conditions consistent.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–20, Phase 3 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: planning a fair test.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: For example, use the same car, ramp surface and release method while changing the height.
misconceptions: Changing several factors at once makes it easier to identify the cause of a change.
topics.question: When testing whether ramp height affects a toy car's travel distance, what should stay the same?
topics.answer: For example, use the same car, ramp surface and release method while changing the height.
topics.explanation: A fair test changes one factor deliberately while measuring an outcome and keeping relevant conditions consistent.
hints: Identify the factor being changed.
Choose another factor that might affect distance and keep it consistent.
topics.activity: Plan a toy-car ramp test and list the changed factor, measured result and two controlled conditions.

topics.name: Adaptations and environment
topics.description: Inherited characteristics can affect how well organisms survive and reproduce in particular environments. The usefulness of a feature depends on conditions.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 21–22, Phase 3 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: adaptations and environment.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They can help the bird push against water when swimming.
misconceptions: Every adaptation guarantees survival in every environment.
topics.question: How could webbed feet help an aquatic bird?
topics.answer: They can help the bird push against water when swimming.
topics.explanation: Inherited characteristics can affect how well organisms survive and reproduce in particular environments. The usefulness of a feature depends on conditions.
hints: What does the bird move through?
How might a broad foot interact with water?
topics.activity: Compare illustrations of two birds' feet and suggest how each structure could help in its environment.

topics.name: Photosynthesis and plant needs
topics.description: Photosynthesis uses light to help plants make sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Plants also respire to release usable energy from food.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 21–22, Phase 3 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: photosynthesis and plant needs.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Light, usually from the Sun.
misconceptions: Plants get all their food by taking it directly from soil.
topics.question: What energy source helps a plant make sugar through photosynthesis?
topics.answer: Light, usually from the Sun.
topics.explanation: Photosynthesis uses light to help plants make sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Plants also respire to release usable energy from food.
hints: Think about what reaches a leaf during daylight.
The process uses light energy.
topics.activity: Draw a simple model with light, water and carbon dioxide entering a plant and sugar being produced.

topics.name: Cells as living structures
topics.description: Cells are basic units of living things. Observations and models can show structures, although a model does not show every detail.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 21–22, Phase 3 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: cells as living structures.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Plant cells.
misconceptions: A model of a cell must show every feature at the same size as reality.
topics.question: A microscope image shows repeated small compartments in a plant leaf. What might they represent?
topics.answer: Plant cells.
topics.explanation: Cells are basic units of living things. Observations and models can show structures, although a model does not show every detail.
hints: What small living units make up plant tissues?
A microscope can reveal units too small to see clearly unaided.
topics.activity: Look at a labelled image of plant cells and compare the image with a simple drawing, noting one limitation of the drawing.

topics.name: Atomic number and elements
topics.description: An element is identified by the number of protons in its atoms. Models describe the nucleus and electrons using evidence.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 24–28, Phase 4 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: atomic number and elements.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Six.
misconceptions: Atomic number counts neutrons rather than protons.
topics.question: An atom has six protons. What is its atomic number?
topics.answer: Six.
topics.explanation: An element is identified by the number of protons in its atoms. Models describe the nucleus and electrons using evidence.
hints: Which particles determine atomic number?
Count the protons.
topics.activity: Use a simple periodic table to locate elements with different atomic numbers and explain what that number represents.

topics.name: Forces and changes in motion
topics.description: A net force can change an object's velocity. The resulting change depends on the total force and the object's mass.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 24–28, Phase 4 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: forces and changes in motion.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Its acceleration can increase, assuming other relevant conditions are unchanged.
misconceptions: A moving object needs a continuous unbalanced force simply to keep a constant velocity.
topics.question: If the same trolley experiences a larger unbalanced push, what change might occur?
topics.answer: Its acceleration can increase, assuming other relevant conditions are unchanged.
topics.explanation: A net force can change an object's velocity. The resulting change depends on the total force and the object's mass.
hints: Compare the size of the unbalanced force.
What happens to the rate at which velocity changes?
topics.activity: Draw two force diagrams for the same trolley and explain the expected difference in acceleration.

topics.name: Complete electrical circuits
topics.description: An electric circuit needs a complete conducting path for current to flow. Circuit components can affect current and energy transfers.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 24–28, Phase 4 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: complete electrical circuits.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The conducting path is broken, so current no longer flows around the circuit.
misconceptions: A bulb lights even when the circuit has a gap.
topics.question: Why does a bulb stop glowing when a simple circuit is opened?
topics.answer: The conducting path is broken, so current no longer flows around the circuit.
topics.explanation: An electric circuit needs a complete conducting path for current to flow. Circuit components can affect current and energy transfers.
hints: Follow the conducting path from one battery terminal.
Is there a complete loop through the bulb?
topics.activity: Draw a battery, switch and bulb in a closed loop; indicate what changes when the switch opens.

topics.name: Cell structures and functions
topics.description: Eukaryotic cells contain structures with different functions. Plant cells have additional structures including a cell wall and chloroplasts.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 29–31, Phase 4 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: cell structures and functions.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The chloroplast.
misconceptions: All cells have exactly the same structures.
topics.question: Which plant-cell structure captures light for photosynthesis?
topics.answer: The chloroplast.
topics.explanation: Eukaryotic cells contain structures with different functions. Plant cells have additional structures including a cell wall and chloroplasts.
hints: Which process uses light to make sugars?
Find the structure associated with that process.
topics.activity: Compare labelled plant and animal cell diagrams and explain one structure found in the plant cell.

topics.name: Inherited variation and selection
topics.description: Individuals in a population vary. If a heritable variation affects survival or reproduction, it may become more or less common over generations.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 29–31, Phase 4 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: inherited variation and selection.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Individuals with that trait may leave more offspring in a particular environment, passing the trait on more often.
misconceptions: An individual chooses a useful trait and passes the acquired change to offspring.
topics.question: Why might a heritable trait become more common over generations?
topics.answer: Individuals with that trait may leave more offspring in a particular environment, passing the trait on more often.
topics.explanation: Individuals in a population vary. If a heritable variation affects survival or reproduction, it may become more or less common over generations.
hints: The trait must be passed to offspring.
Think about differences in survival and reproduction over many generations.
topics.activity: Use coloured counters to model a fictional population over several generations and discuss where the model simplifies real biology.

topics.name: Pathogens & the Immune System
topics.description: Infectious diseases can be caused by pathogens. The body has barriers and immune responses that help protect against disease.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 29–31, Phase 4 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: pathogens and immune defences.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It provides a physical barrier that can limit entry of pathogens.
misconceptions: All diseases are infectious and spread between people.
topics.question: How can intact skin help protect against pathogens?
topics.answer: It provides a physical barrier that can limit entry of pathogens.
topics.explanation: Infectious diseases can be caused by pathogens. The body has barriers and immune responses that help protect against disease.
hints: Think of the body's outer covering.
How could a barrier prevent entry?
topics.activity: Draw a simple diagram distinguishing an outer barrier from an immune response inside the body; use a reliable health source.

topics.name: Absorbent and waterproof materials
topics.description: Materials differ in how readily they let water soak in or pass through them; this affects their uses.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 9–10, Phase 1 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: absorbent and waterproof materials.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can help stop water passing through to the object underneath.
misconceptions: Every material absorbs water in the same way.
topics.question: Why might a waterproof cover be useful in rain?
topics.answer: It can help stop water passing through to the object underneath.
topics.explanation: Materials differ in how readily they let water soak in or pass through them; this affects their uses.
hints: What happens to rain on the cover?
Does the material let water pass through easily?
topics.activity: Place a small drop of water on safe samples of paper and plastic and observe what happens.

topics.name: Surfaces and moving objects
topics.description: The surfaces touching an object can affect how easily it moves across them.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 9–10, Phase 1 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: surfaces and moving objects.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The surfaces interact differently with the toy and can oppose movement by different amounts.
misconceptions: The surface beneath an object never affects its movement.
topics.question: Why might a toy slide differently on a smooth table and a soft rug?
topics.answer: The surfaces interact differently with the toy and can oppose movement by different amounts.
topics.explanation: The surfaces touching an object can affect how easily it moves across them.
hints: Compare the two surfaces.
Which might resist sliding more?
topics.activity: Gently slide the same object across two safe surfaces and describe the differences.

topics.name: Simple Food Chains
topics.description: A food chain represents a feeding relationship and shows how organisms depend on a source of food.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 11–12, Phase 1 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: a simple food chain.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The grass or other plant material in this model.
misconceptions: A food-chain arrow only shows where an animal lives.
topics.question: In a simple chain grass → insect → bird, what does the insect eat?
topics.answer: The grass or other plant material in this model.
topics.explanation: A food chain represents a feeding relationship and shows how organisms depend on a source of food.
hints: Follow the arrow from the grass.
Which organism is shown receiving food from the grass?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional three-organism chain and explain what each arrow represents.

topics.name: Observing living things safely
topics.description: Observations use senses or tools to notice and record features. Some organisms should be observed without touching or disturbing them.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 11–12, Phase 1 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: observing living things safely.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Some fungi may be harmful, and observation can be made safely from a distance.
misconceptions: Every organism found outdoors is safe to touch.
topics.question: Why should a learner observe an unknown mushroom without handling it?
topics.answer: Some fungi may be harmful, and observation can be made safely from a distance.
topics.explanation: Observations use senses or tools to notice and record features. Some organisms should be observed without touching or disturbing them.
hints: Is it always safe to touch an unknown organism?
What can be recorded without touching it?
topics.activity: Observe a photograph of an unfamiliar organism and record its colour and shape without guessing that it is safe.

topics.name: Magnetic forces
topics.description: Magnets can exert forces without touching an object, but not every material is attracted to a magnet.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 14–15, Phase 2 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: magnetic forces.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: No. Wood is not generally attracted to a magnet.
misconceptions: Magnets attract every kind of material.
topics.question: Will a magnet necessarily attract a wooden block?
topics.answer: No. Wood is not generally attracted to a magnet.
topics.explanation: Magnets can exert forces without touching an object, but not every material is attracted to a magnet.
hints: Think about what the block is made from.
Are all materials magnetic?
topics.activity: With a small safe magnet, test a selection of everyday objects and record which are attracted.

topics.name: Gravity & Falling Objects
topics.description: Gravity is an attractive force that can act without contact. Near Earth it contributes to objects falling towards the ground.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 14–15, Phase 2 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: gravity and falling objects.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Gravity.
misconceptions: A force can only act when two objects are touching.
topics.question: What force helps explain why a dropped object falls towards the ground?
topics.answer: Gravity.
topics.explanation: Gravity is an attractive force that can act without contact. Near Earth it contributes to objects falling towards the ground.
hints: Which direction does the object move?
What attracts objects towards Earth?
topics.activity: Observe a light, safe object being dropped over a short distance and describe its motion.

topics.name: Thermal energy and temperature
topics.description: Heating and cooling can transfer energy and change temperature or state; temperature and the amount of thermal energy are related but distinct ideas.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 14–15, Phase 2 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: thermal energy and temperature.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Energy is transferred from the warmer surroundings to the ice, allowing it to melt.
misconceptions: Cold is a substance that flows from ice into a room.
topics.question: Why might an ice cube melt in a warmer room?
topics.answer: Energy is transferred from the warmer surroundings to the ice, allowing it to melt.
topics.explanation: Heating and cooling can transfer energy and change temperature or state; temperature and the amount of thermal energy are related but distinct ideas.
hints: Compare the temperatures of the ice and room.
In which direction can energy be transferred?
topics.activity: Watch ice melt in a dish at room temperature and describe the change without touching hot equipment.

topics.name: Building a simple circuit
topics.description: A simple circuit connects a power source and components in a conducting loop. A gap can interrupt the path.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 14–15, Phase 2 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: a simple circuit.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The circuit does not yet provide a complete conducting loop through the bulb.
misconceptions: One connection to a battery always makes a complete circuit.
topics.question: A battery and bulb are connected by only one wire. Why might the bulb not light?
topics.answer: The circuit does not yet provide a complete conducting loop through the bulb.
topics.explanation: A simple circuit connects a power source and components in a conducting loop. A gap can interrupt the path.
hints: Trace the path from one battery terminal.
Does it return to the other terminal through the bulb?
topics.activity: Draw a battery, bulb and two connecting paths to show a complete loop; use only low-voltage equipment with supervision if building it.

topics.name: Skeletons and support
topics.description: Many animals have internal skeletons; others have an external skeleton or no rigid skeleton. Structures help support and protect the body.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 16–17, Phase 2 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: skeletons and support.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can support the body, protect organs or work with muscles to enable movement.
misconceptions: All animals have the same internal skeleton.
topics.question: What is one function of a skeleton in a vertebrate?
topics.answer: It can support the body, protect organs or work with muscles to enable movement.
topics.explanation: Many animals have internal skeletons; others have an external skeleton or no rigid skeleton. Structures help support and protect the body.
hints: Think about what supports the body.
Some bones protect important organs.
topics.activity: Compare labelled diagrams of a vertebrate and an invertebrate and note one difference in support.

topics.name: Digestion and nutrients
topics.description: The digestive system helps break down food and absorb nutrients that the body can use.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 16–17, Phase 2 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: digestion and nutrients.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It breaks food down so nutrients can be absorbed and used by the body.
misconceptions: Food reaches every part of the body without being broken down.
topics.question: What is one purpose of digestion?
topics.answer: It breaks food down so nutrients can be absorbed and used by the body.
topics.explanation: The digestive system helps break down food and absorb nutrients that the body can use.
hints: What happens to food after it is eaten?
How can useful substances become available to the body?
topics.activity: Use a labelled diagram to trace a simple path through the digestive system and explain one stage.

topics.name: Speed, distance and time
topics.description: Average speed relates the distance travelled to the time taken over a chosen interval.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–20, Phase 3 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: speed, distance and time.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: 4 metres per second.
misconceptions: Speed is found by multiplying distance by time.
topics.question: A cyclist travels 12 metres in 3 seconds. What is the average speed?
topics.answer: 4 metres per second.
topics.explanation: Average speed relates the distance travelled to the time taken over a chosen interval.
hints: Divide distance by time.
Twelve divided by three is four.
topics.activity: Use fictional distances and times to calculate average speed for two journeys, keeping the units visible.

topics.name: Levers and turning effects
topics.description: The turning effect of a force depends on its size and distance from a pivot. A balanced lever has equal opposing turning effects.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–20, Phase 3 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: levers and turning effects.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The lighter person could sit farther from the pivot, subject to the actual forces and distances.
misconceptions: A seesaw can only balance when both sides have equal masses at any distance.
topics.question: How could a lighter person balance a heavier person on a seesaw?
topics.answer: The lighter person could sit farther from the pivot, subject to the actual forces and distances.
topics.explanation: The turning effect of a force depends on its size and distance from a pivot. A balanced lever has equal opposing turning effects.
hints: Compare the distances from the pivot.
Can a longer distance increase a turning effect?
topics.activity: Draw a seesaw model and compare two fictional force-and-distance combinations; do not attempt unsafe balancing.

topics.name: Earth's rotation and day/night
topics.description: Earth's rotation causes places to move into and out of sunlight, producing a day–night cycle.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–20, Phase 3 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: earth's rotation and day and night.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The place is on the side of Earth facing away from the Sun.
misconceptions: Night happens because the Sun is turned off.
topics.question: Why does a place experience night in a simple Earth–Sun model?
topics.answer: The place is on the side of Earth facing away from the Sun.
topics.explanation: Earth's rotation causes places to move into and out of sunlight, producing a day–night cycle.
hints: Imagine a rotating ball and a fixed light source.
Which side is not receiving direct light?
topics.activity: Use a ball and a stationary torch to model day and night, then state one way the model differs from reality.

topics.name: Solutions and dissolving
topics.description: A solution forms when a soluble substance dissolves in a solvent. Dissolved material is still present even when it is not visible.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 19–20, Phase 3 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: solutions and dissolving.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: No. It is dispersed in the solution and is still present.
misconceptions: Dissolving destroys the material that dissolves.
topics.question: When salt dissolves in water, has the salt disappeared?
topics.answer: No. It is dispersed in the solution and is still present.
topics.explanation: A solution forms when a soluble substance dissolves in a solvent. Dissolved material is still present even when it is not visible.
hints: Can the salt be recovered by removing water?
Not being visible is different from not existing.
topics.activity: Stir a small amount of salt into water and discuss how evaporation could provide evidence that salt remains.

topics.name: Cells, Tissues & Organs
topics.description: In multicellular organisms, cells can form tissues, tissues can form organs, and organs can work together in systems.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 21–22, Phase 3 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: cells, tissues and organs.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: An organ is made from tissues.
misconceptions: Cells are made from organs rather than the other way around.
topics.question: Which is generally made from tissues: an organ or an individual cell?
topics.answer: An organ is made from tissues.
topics.explanation: In multicellular organisms, cells can form tissues, tissues can form organs, and organs can work together in systems.
hints: Begin with cells as smaller units.
What can a group of tissues form?
topics.activity: Arrange cards labelled cell, tissue, organ and system from smaller to larger and give one familiar example.

topics.name: Living and non-living ecosystem factors
topics.description: An ecosystem includes organisms interacting with each other and with non-living conditions such as water, light and temperature.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 21–22, Phase 3 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: living and non-living ecosystem factors.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Water temperature is a non-living factor; the fish is living.
misconceptions: An ecosystem contains only living things.
topics.question: In a pond, which is a non-living factor: a fish or water temperature?
topics.answer: Water temperature is a non-living factor; the fish is living.
topics.explanation: An ecosystem includes organisms interacting with each other and with non-living conditions such as water, light and temperature.
hints: Which item is an organism?
Which describes a physical condition?
topics.activity: Make two lists for a fictional pond: living organisms and non-living conditions, then describe one interaction.

topics.name: Acids, bases and the pH scale
topics.description: The pH scale describes how acidic or alkaline a solution is; for typical aqueous solutions, pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 24–28, Phase 4 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: acids, bases and the ph scale.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It is acidic.
misconceptions: A lower pH always means a solution is more alkaline.
topics.question: A solution has pH 3. Is it acidic or alkaline?
topics.answer: It is acidic.
topics.explanation: The pH scale describes how acidic or alkaline a solution is; for typical aqueous solutions, pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline.
hints: Compare 3 with neutral pH 7.
A value below 7 indicates an acid.
topics.activity: Classify fictional pH values on a number line; do not taste or handle unknown chemicals.

topics.name: Series vs parallel circuits
topics.description: A series circuit has one path for current; a parallel circuit has multiple branches. A break affects the paths differently.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 24–28, Phase 4 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: series and parallel circuit paths.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The other complete branch can still carry current if the source and its path remain intact.
misconceptions: All branches of a parallel circuit must stop conducting whenever one branch is opened.
topics.question: In a simple parallel circuit, what happens to another complete branch if one branch is opened?
topics.answer: The other complete branch can still carry current if the source and its path remain intact.
topics.explanation: A series circuit has one path for current; a parallel circuit has multiple branches. A break affects the paths differently.
hints: How many paths are available?
Does the other branch still form a complete path?
topics.activity: Draw series and parallel circuits and mark which path is interrupted by an opened switch.

topics.name: Pressure, force and area
topics.description: Pressure is force distributed over an area. For the same perpendicular force, a smaller contact area produces greater pressure.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 24–28, Phase 4 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: pressure, force and area.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Pressure increases.
misconceptions: For the same force, a smaller area always produces less pressure.
topics.question: If the same force acts on a smaller area, what happens to pressure?
topics.answer: Pressure increases.
topics.explanation: Pressure is force distributed over an area. For the same perpendicular force, a smaller contact area produces greater pressure.
hints: Use pressure = force divided by area.
What happens to a quotient when the denominator decreases and the numerator stays fixed?
topics.activity: Compare fictional force-and-area pairs using simple numbers and include units.

topics.name: Interpreting a position–time graph
topics.description: A position–time graph represents position over time; the slope of a straight section describes velocity along the chosen axis.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 24–28, Phase 4 > Physical Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: interpreting a position–time graph.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Position is not changing during that interval, so velocity is zero.
misconceptions: A horizontal position–time graph means the object is moving at a high constant speed.
topics.question: On a position–time graph, what does a horizontal section indicate?
topics.answer: Position is not changing during that interval, so velocity is zero.
topics.explanation: A position–time graph represents position over time; the slope of a straight section describes velocity along the chosen axis.
hints: Does the vertical value change as time passes?
What does unchanged position mean for motion?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional graph for moving, stopping and moving again, then describe each section.

topics.name: Diffusion in biological systems
topics.description: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration. It helps explain movement of gases in biological systems.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 29–31, Phase 4 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: diffusion in biological systems.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: From higher concentration towards lower concentration.
misconceptions: Diffusion requires every particle to move in the same direction at every moment.
topics.question: Which way is net diffusion expected between higher and lower concentration regions?
topics.answer: From higher concentration towards lower concentration.
topics.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration. It helps explain movement of gases in biological systems.
hints: Compare the two concentrations.
Which direction reduces the concentration difference?
topics.activity: Use dots on paper to model particles spreading between two areas and identify a limitation of the model.

topics.name: Aerobic Respiration
topics.description: In aerobic cellular respiration, cells use glucose and oxygen to release energy for life processes, producing carbon dioxide and water.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 29–31, Phase 4 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: cellular respiration.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Glucose and oxygen.
misconceptions: Respiration and photosynthesis are the same process.
topics.question: What two inputs are used in aerobic cellular respiration?
topics.answer: Glucose and oxygen.
topics.explanation: In aerobic cellular respiration, cells use glucose and oxygen to release energy for life processes, producing carbon dioxide and water.
hints: One input is a sugar.
The other is a gas obtained through breathing in humans.
topics.activity: Draw a labelled model of inputs and outputs for aerobic respiration and compare it with photosynthesis.

topics.name: Water and ecosystems
topics.description: Water moves through ecosystems and supports organisms, soils and biological processes. Availability can affect where organisms live.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 29–31, Phase 4 > Biological Science; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: water and ecosystems.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Organisms and processes depend on water, so a change can alter the conditions and resources available.
misconceptions: Water availability has no effect on living things.
topics.question: Why might a change in freshwater availability affect an ecosystem?
topics.answer: Organisms and processes depend on water, so a change can alter the conditions and resources available.
topics.explanation: Water moves through ecosystems and supports organisms, soils and biological processes. Availability can affect where organisms live.
hints: What uses water in the ecosystem?
How might less water affect plants or other organisms?
topics.activity: Use a fictional catchment diagram to trace water through soil, plants and the atmosphere.

topics.name: How Shadows Form
topics.description: A shadow appears when an object blocks light travelling from a source to a surface.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Physical Science > Year 1 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply how shadows form using an example.
evidence: Identifies the object blocking the light and the surface where the shadow appears.
misconceptions: A shadow is a coloured substance that an object gives off.
topics.question: A torch shines on a wall with a book between them. Why is there a dark shape on the wall?
topics.answer: The book blocks some of the torchlight.
topics.explanation: Less light reaches the part of the wall behind the book, making a shadow.
hints: Trace the path from torch to wall.
What is between the torch and the wall?
topics.activity: With a torch, card and wall, move the card and observe its shadow. Never look directly at the Sun.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Pitch of Sounds
topics.description: Pitch describes how high or low a sound seems and relates to how quickly its source vibrates.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Physical Science > Year 2 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply pitch of sounds using an example.
evidence: Distinguishes a higher vibration frequency from a louder sound.
misconceptions: A louder sound always has a higher pitch.
topics.question: Two whistles are equally loud. Which has a higher pitch if one vibrates faster?
topics.answer: The whistle that vibrates faster.
topics.explanation: A higher vibration frequency produces a higher pitch, while loudness is a separate property.
hints: Think about how quickly the source moves back and forth.
Compare vibration speed rather than volume.
topics.activity: Pluck a short and a long stretched rubber band gently and describe the different pitches; keep both away from eyes.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Transparent and opaque materials
topics.description: Materials differ in how much light they let through: transparent materials transmit most light, while opaque materials block it.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Physical Science > Year 3 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply transparent and opaque materials using an example.
evidence: Uses the behaviour of light to compare two materials.
misconceptions: Every material either lets all light through or blocks all of it.
topics.question: Why can a clear window let us see outside but a cardboard sheet cannot?
topics.answer: The clear window lets most light through; the cardboard blocks it.
topics.explanation: Light reaches our eyes through the transparent window, while opaque cardboard absorbs or reflects it.
hints: Think about how much light passes through each material.
Which one blocks the light?
topics.activity: Shine a small torch at clear plastic, thin paper and cardboard and compare the light reaching a wall.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Sunlight and moonlight
topics.description: The Sun emits light; the Moon can be seen because it reflects sunlight.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Physical Science > Year 3 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply sunlight and moonlight using an example.
evidence: Explains where the light reaching us from the Moon comes from.
misconceptions: The Moon is a star that produces its own light.
topics.question: Where does the light that lets us see the Moon come from?
topics.answer: It comes from the Sun and is reflected by the Moon.
topics.explanation: Sunlight falls on the Moon and some of that light reaches our eyes.
hints: Which object is a light source?
The Moon reflects light from a nearby star.
topics.activity: Use a torch and a ball to model sunlight reflecting from the Moon; never look directly at the Sun.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Measuring temperature
topics.description: A thermometer measures how hot or cold something is, often using degrees Celsius.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 4 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply measuring temperature using an example.
evidence: Reads and compares Celsius temperatures without confusing temperature and amount.
misconceptions: A bigger cup of water must have a higher temperature than a smaller cup.
topics.question: One cup of water is 18°C and another is 25°C. Which is warmer?
topics.answer: The water at 25°C.
topics.explanation: A higher reading on the same Celsius scale indicates a higher temperature.
hints: Compare the two readings.
Which number is larger?
topics.activity: Draw two thermometer scales labelled 18°C and 25°C and mark the warmer one.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Magnetic poles
topics.description: A magnet has north and south poles; unlike poles attract and like poles repel.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 4 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply magnetic poles using an example.
evidence: Predicts attraction or repulsion between two labelled poles.
misconceptions: Every pair of magnetic poles attracts.
topics.question: What happens when the north poles of two magnets are brought close together?
topics.answer: They repel each other.
topics.explanation: Like magnetic poles repel; a north pole and a south pole attract.
hints: Look at the labels on both ends.
Are the two poles alike or unlike?
topics.activity: With two classroom magnets, test like and unlike poles and draw arrows for what happens.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Density and floating
topics.description: Density compares mass with volume; an object less dense than the surrounding liquid floats.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 5 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply density and floating using an example.
evidence: Uses density values in the same units to predict floating.
misconceptions: The heavier object always sinks regardless of its size and volume.
topics.question: A solid has density 0.7 g/mL and water has density 1.0 g/mL. Will the solid float in water?
topics.answer: It will float.
topics.explanation: The solid is less dense than the water it displaces.
hints: Compare 0.7 with 1.0.
The solid is less dense than water.
topics.activity: Place safe sealed objects in a basin of water and compare predictions with observations; dry spills promptly.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Why We Have Seasons
topics.description: Earth's tilted axis changes the angle and duration of sunlight a region receives during its orbit.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 5 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply earth's tilt and the seasons using an example.
evidence: Connects seasonal daylight and sunlight angle to Earth's tilt.
misconceptions: The Southern Hemisphere has summer because Earth is much closer to the Sun then.
topics.question: Why does the Southern Hemisphere receive longer days in its summer?
topics.answer: Its tilt points that hemisphere more towards the Sun during that part of Earth's orbit.
topics.explanation: Tilt changes both the angle of sunlight and the length of the daylight period.
hints: Think about the direction of Earth's axis.
Which hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun?
topics.activity: Model Earth with a tilted ball around a stationary torch and compare the lit regions.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Plant Reproduction
topics.description: Flowers support reproduction: pollination can lead to fertilisation, followed by seed development.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 4 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply plant reproduction using an example.
evidence: Describes the connection between a flower and the seeds in a fruit.
misconceptions: A fruit and its seeds appear without a flower or fertilisation.
topics.question: What can develop after a flower is pollinated and fertilised?
topics.answer: Seeds can develop, and the flower can develop into a fruit containing them.
topics.explanation: Flowering plants reproduce using structures in flowers; fertilisation enables seed development.
hints: Start with the flower.
What structure can later contain the new seeds?
topics.activity: Observe a flower and a cut fruit with an adult and draw where their structures are; wash hands afterwards.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Classification Keys
topics.description: A classification key identifies an organism by following choices based on observable features.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 5 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply classification keys using an example.
evidence: Uses a simple observable feature to separate two kinds of organisms.
misconceptions: An organism can only be classified by where it lives.
topics.question: A key first asks whether an animal has six legs. Which group does a pictured animal with six legs follow?
topics.answer: The six-legged group.
topics.explanation: A classification key sorts by a stated feature at each decision point.
hints: Count the legs in the description.
Choose the branch that matches six legs.
topics.activity: Draw a two-choice key for pictures of four familiar animals using visible features.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Fungi as a distinct group
topics.description: Fungi include mushrooms, moulds and yeasts, and form a group separate from plants and animals.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 5 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply fungi as a distinct group using an example.
evidence: Identifies fungi without assuming a mushroom is a plant.
misconceptions: Mushrooms are plants because they grow in the ground.
topics.question: Is a mushroom a plant, an animal or a fungus?
topics.answer: It is a fungus.
topics.explanation: Fungi form their own group and do not need to be plants simply because they grow in soil.
hints: A mushroom belongs with mould and yeast.
Which of the three groups includes moulds and yeasts?
topics.activity: Sort pictures of plants, animals and fungi; never touch or taste unknown mushrooms.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: The Circulatory System
topics.description: The heart pumps blood through vessels, carrying absorbed nutrients and water around the body.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply the circulatory system using an example.
evidence: Describes the heart's role in moving blood and nutrients.
misconceptions: Food passes directly through blood vessels without digestion.
topics.question: How do nutrients absorbed from the intestine reach other parts of the body?
topics.answer: The bloodstream carries them as the heart pumps blood around the body.
topics.explanation: Nutrients enter the blood mainly through the intestine, and blood vessels connect the intestine with body tissues.
hints: Which fluid travels around the body?
What pumps that fluid?
topics.activity: Draw a simple arrow diagram from intestine to blood to a muscle.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Inheritance and environmental effects
topics.description: Offspring inherit traits from parents, while conditions in the environment can also affect how some traits develop.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply inheritance and environmental effects using an example.
evidence: Gives one inherited influence and one environmental influence on an organism's features.
misconceptions: All visible differences are inherited and the environment makes no difference.
topics.question: Two genetically similar plants grow differently because one receives less water. What additional influence could explain this?
topics.answer: The difference in water available to the plants.
topics.explanation: Environment can influence growth even when plants share inherited features.
hints: Compare the plants' growing conditions.
Which resource differs?
topics.activity: Draw two plants with different watering conditions and explain a possible difference in growth.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Physical vs Chemical Changes
topics.description: A physical change alters form or state; a chemical change makes one or more new substances.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply physical vs chemical changes using an example.
evidence: Distinguishes melting from a change that forms new substances.
misconceptions: Every change in appearance means a chemical reaction has occurred.
topics.question: Is melting an ice cube a physical or a chemical change?
topics.answer: It is a physical change.
topics.explanation: The water changes state but remains the same substance; no new substance is formed.
hints: What is the ice made of before and after melting?
Does a new substance form?
topics.activity: Let ice melt in a bowl and describe what has changed and what has stayed the same.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Showing forces with arrows
topics.description: A force has a direction and size and can be represented with an arrow.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply showing forces with arrows using an example.
evidence: Uses arrow direction and relative length to represent two forces.
misconceptions: A force arrow only tells which way an object moves.
topics.question: In a force diagram, how can you show a larger rightward push than another rightward push?
topics.answer: Draw a longer arrow pointing right for the larger push.
topics.explanation: Arrow direction shows the direction of the force and relative arrow length shows its size.
hints: Both pushes point the same way.
Change the length of one arrow.
topics.activity: Draw a box with a small leftward arrow and a larger rightward arrow, and label each push.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Moon Phases
topics.description: The Moon orbits Earth, and its changing position affects how much of its sunlit half we see.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 7 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply moon phases and reflected sunlight using an example.
evidence: Explains a Moon phase using the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon.
misconceptions: The changing phases are caused by Earth's shadow covering the Moon each month.
topics.question: Why can the visible shape of the Moon appear to change during a month?
topics.answer: We see different portions of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
topics.explanation: The Moon's illuminated half remains lit by the Sun, but the angle from Earth changes.
hints: The Moon reflects sunlight.
Think about how our view changes as the Moon moves.
topics.activity: Use a torch, ball and observer to model different views of the lit half of the Moon.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Heating and particle motion
topics.description: Heating a material transfers energy to its particles; their movement changes as its temperature changes.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 7 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply heating and particle motion using an example.
evidence: Relates increased particle movement to a rise in temperature.
misconceptions: The particles in a solid disappear when it becomes liquid.
topics.question: What happens to particle motion when a sample of liquid is warmed?
topics.answer: On average, its particles move faster.
topics.explanation: Energy transferred to the material increases the particles' average kinetic energy.
hints: Think about the particles' movement.
Does their movement speed up or stop?
topics.activity: Draw particle diagrams for the same liquid before and after warming, using arrows to show motion.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Refraction of light
topics.description: Light can change direction when it passes between materials in which it travels at different speeds.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply refraction of light using an example.
evidence: Explains why an object viewed through water may appear displaced.
misconceptions: A straw in water really breaks where it enters the water.
topics.question: Why does a straight straw in a clear glass of water seem bent?
topics.answer: Light changes direction as it passes between the water and air.
topics.explanation: Refraction changes the path of light reaching the eye, making the underwater part appear shifted.
hints: Follow light from the straw through water and air.
What changes when light enters a different material?
topics.activity: Place a straw in a clear glass of water and draw both its actual shape and its apparent shape.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Concentration of solutions
topics.description: Concentration compares the amount of solute with the amount of solution.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply concentration of solutions using an example.
evidence: Compares solutions with the same volume when they contain different amounts of dissolved material.
misconceptions: All clear solutions have the same concentration.
topics.question: Two equal-sized cups contain dissolved sugar. One has one teaspoon and the other has two. Which is more concentrated?
topics.answer: The cup with two teaspoons, assuming all the sugar dissolves.
topics.explanation: The same volume of solution contains more dissolved sugar.
hints: The volumes are the same.
Which cup contains more dissolved sugar?
topics.activity: Use labelled drawings of equal cups and different amounts of dissolved solute to compare concentration.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: How rocks form
topics.description: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form through different processes such as cooling, deposition and heat or pressure.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply how rocks form using an example.
evidence: Matches a rock type with a plausible formation process.
misconceptions: All rocks form when molten material cools.
topics.question: What kind of rock forms when molten rock cools and solidifies?
topics.answer: Igneous rock.
topics.explanation: Cooling and solidification of molten material produce igneous rocks; other rock types have different formation processes.
hints: Think about melted rock.
Which rock group forms on cooling?
topics.activity: Make three labelled sketches showing cooling, layers of sediment, and a rock changed by heat and pressure.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Sexual and asexual reproduction
topics.description: Asexual reproduction can produce offspring from one parent; sexual reproduction involves combining genetic material from parents.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Biological Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply sexual and asexual reproduction using an example.
evidence: Distinguishes one-parent reproduction from reproduction involving two gametes.
misconceptions: Every living thing needs two parents to reproduce.
topics.question: A new plant grows from a stem cutting. Is this sexual or asexual reproduction?
topics.answer: Asexual reproduction.
topics.explanation: The new plant grows from part of one parent without the fusion of gametes.
hints: How many parent plants supplied the cutting?
Were gametes combined?
topics.activity: Sketch how a healthy plant cutting could grow new roots, without removing plants from public places.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: How Natural Selection Works
topics.description: Heritable differences can affect survival and reproduction, so a population may change across generations.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Biological Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply variation and natural selection using an example.
evidence: Explains change in a population by differences in inherited traits and reproduction.
misconceptions: An individual changes its inherited traits because it needs to survive.
topics.question: If birds with an inherited beak shape obtain more food and leave more offspring, what may happen over generations?
topics.answer: That beak shape may become more common in the population.
topics.explanation: Individuals with that inherited variation may contribute more offspring to later generations.
hints: Think about which birds leave more offspring.
What happens to a heritable trait carried by more parents?
topics.activity: Use two coloured counters for inherited variants and model different reproduction over several generations.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Symbiosis
topics.description: Organisms can interact in ways that benefit both partners, benefit one while harming the other, or affect them differently.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Biological Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply relationships between organisms using an example.
evidence: Compares the effects of a relationship on each organism.
misconceptions: All close relationships between species benefit both participants.
topics.question: A parasite obtains nutrients from a host and harms it. Who benefits?
topics.answer: The parasite benefits, while the host is harmed.
topics.explanation: The effect on each partner helps classify the interaction; close contact alone does not mean mutual benefit.
hints: Consider the two organisms separately.
Which gains nutrients and which is harmed?
topics.activity: Create a two-column chart for the effects of a parasite and pollinator on their partners.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: The Periodic Table
topics.description: The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number and groups elements with related properties.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply the periodic table using an example.
evidence: Uses an element's atomic number to identify its position in the sequence.
misconceptions: Elements in the periodic table are arranged alphabetically.
topics.question: What number determines the order of elements in the modern periodic table?
topics.answer: The atomic number.
topics.explanation: Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom and increases across the table.
hints: Think about the number of protons.
The table uses atomic number.
topics.activity: Use a periodic table to find three consecutive atomic numbers and list their element symbols.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Atoms, Elements & Compounds
topics.description: A compound contains atoms of different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply atoms, elements and compounds using an example.
evidence: Distinguishes a compound from a sample containing only one element.
misconceptions: A molecule made of different atoms is an element.
topics.question: Water contains hydrogen and oxygen chemically bonded together. Is water an element or a compound?
topics.answer: A compound.
topics.explanation: Its molecules contain atoms of more than one element bonded together.
hints: Count the different element names.
What do we call different elements chemically bonded?
topics.activity: Draw a labelled water molecule with two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Neutralisation reactions
topics.description: An acid and a base can react to form a salt and water in a neutralisation reaction.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply neutralisation reactions using an example.
evidence: Identifies the kinds of reactants and common products in neutralisation.
misconceptions: Mixing an acid with a base always produces more acid.
topics.question: What reaction occurs when an acid and a base react to form salt and water?
topics.answer: Neutralisation.
topics.explanation: The acid and base react to produce new substances, including a salt and water.
hints: Identify both starting substances.
They are an acid and a base.
topics.activity: Write a word equation for an acid reacting with a base; do not mix household chemicals.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Waves transfer energy
topics.description: Waves can carry energy from place to place without transporting the material of the medium the same distance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply waves transfer energy using an example.
evidence: Explains that a wave transfers energy while particles can oscillate locally.
misconceptions: Water in every wave travels all the way across the ocean with the wave.
topics.question: When a wave passes a floating marker, what can travel across the water while the marker mainly moves locally?
topics.answer: Energy travels with the wave.
topics.explanation: The disturbance travels through the water while nearby water and the marker mostly oscillate around their positions.
hints: Watch the wave travel and the marker move.
Which one carries energy across the water?
topics.activity: Draw successive wave positions and a floating marker moving mainly up and down.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Pressure in liquids
topics.description: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because more liquid is above a deeper point.
topics.locator: PDF p. 27, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply pressure in liquids using an example.
evidence: Compares pressure at different depths in the same liquid.
misconceptions: Liquid pressure is the same at every depth.
topics.question: In a still tank of water, is pressure greater 10 cm or 50 cm below the surface?
topics.answer: It is greater 50 cm below the surface.
topics.explanation: A deeper point has a taller column of water above it, producing greater pressure.
hints: Compare the depths.
Which point has more water above it?
topics.activity: Draw a tank with arrows showing larger pressure at a deeper position.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Buoyant force
topics.description: A fluid exerts an upward buoyant force on an object placed in it.
topics.locator: PDF p. 27, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply buoyant force using an example.
evidence: Identifies the direction of the buoyant force on an object in water.
misconceptions: Water pushes on a submerged object only downwards.
topics.question: In which direction does the buoyant force act on a block in water?
topics.answer: Upwards.
topics.explanation: The surrounding water exerts pressure on the block, producing a net upward force.
hints: Consider the force that helps a boat float.
Does it act up or down?
topics.activity: Draw a block in water with an upward buoyancy arrow and a downward weight arrow.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Tectonic Plates
topics.description: Earth's outer layer is divided into plates that move and interact at their boundaries.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain or apply moving tectonic plates using an example.
evidence: Relates some earthquakes and mountain building to movement at plate boundaries.
misconceptions: Continents and the ocean floor never move.
topics.question: Why are many earthquakes found near tectonic plate boundaries?
topics.answer: Plates move and interact there, releasing energy when rocks slip.
topics.explanation: Plate movement can build stress in rocks; sudden movement can produce earthquakes.
hints: Think about where plates meet.
What can happen when movement suddenly releases stored stress?
topics.activity: Slide two pieces of paper past each other to model a plate boundary; label the model's limitations.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Chromosomes, Genes & DNA
topics.description: Genes are sections of DNA carried on chromosomes and contribute to inherited characteristics.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 knowledge
